newsitem.title: UK: UK stock market seen sturdiest in Western Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK stock market seen sturdiest in Western Europe.

text.p: Britain's stock market looks to be the best placed in western Europe to weather further declines in global equities, strategists said on Monday.

A favourable UK interest rate environment and a breather in a sterling rally which cut the earnings of big overseas earners, should allow the FTSE 100 index of top companies to outperform continental Europe the next few months.

The rest of western Europe is vulnerable after scorching performances in the first half of this year, and because of the fear of a German interest rate hike, maybe as early as this week, analysts said.

On Monday, the FTSE 100 traded 30.3 points lower at 4,835.5 by 1239 GMT. But the blue-chip index clawed back from a day's low of 4,779.3, after a 2.5 percent selloff on Friday, as investors braced for the open on Wall Street.
"It's a nasty situation for the continental markets," said Ian Scott, UK equity strategist at Lehman Brothers.
"I think the FTSE is one of the better placed markets around the world...and valuations on the London market are not stretched like on the continent," he said.
On a price/earnings ratio, London is trading at about 16 times 1998 earnings, versus 18-20 for some European markets, he said.
A six percent sell-off the last two weeks in the FTSE 100, from its record high of 5,095.3, was viewed as a much-needed correction triggered by the Dow's drop on Friday, sources said.
The UK index had gained 24 percent this year to that all-time best, underperforming some other European markets.
In the first six months of this year, the UK market gained about 12 percent, versus more sparkling returns from France, up 23 percent, Germany, 30 percent, and Italy, 25 percent.

"In terms of adding new money, I think that you'd be wary of the European markets...which still look net overvalued against their key fundamental drivers," said Tim O'Dell, international strategist at UBS.
"On a relative basis, the UK looks more attractive, but nowhere do the stock markets in Europe or the U.S. look cheap," he said.
On Monday, with some markets reopening from a holiday on Friday, European share prices also buckled.
By midday, though, bargain hunting had emerged, with Dutch, French and German shares, to name a few, bouncing from their early tumble.
In a reversal of fortunes this month, UK shares have clung onto expectations for interest rates to stay on hold for the time being.

After four rate hikes in the past four months, culminating with a move to 7.0 percent from 6.75 percent in early August, the Bank of England said rates have "reached a level consistent with the inflation target."

"With the FTSE down below 4,800 after being up toward 5,100, I can't get too bearish," one trader said. "There are worries about German interest rates...but we have had our interest rate (increases)."
